sectionTitle: Use of amount of substance in relation to masses of pure substances

specStatements.text: Chemical amounts are measured in moles. The symbol for the unit mole is mol.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass.
One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles, atoms, molecules or ions as one mole of any other substance.
The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance is the Avogadro constant. The value of the Avogadro constant is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole.

Students should understand that the measurement of amounts in moles can apply to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae and equations, for example that in one mole of carbon (C) the number of atoms is the same as the number of molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂ ).
Students should be able to use the relative formula mass of a substance to calculate the number of moles in a given mass of that substance and vice versa.
The masses of reactants and products can be calculated from balanced symbol equations.
Chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of moles. For example:
Mg +2HCI →MgCI₂+ H₂
shows that one mole of magnesium reacts with two moles of hydrochloric acid to produce one mole of magnesium chloride and one mole of hydrogen gas.
Students should be able to:
calculate the masses of substances shown in a balanced symbol equation
calculate the masses of reactants and products from the balanced symbol equation and the mass of a given reactant or product.

The balancing numbers in a symbol equation can be calculated from the masses of reactants and products by converting the masses in grams to amounts in moles and converting the numbers of moles to simple whole number ratios.
Students should be able to balance an equation given the masses of reactants and products.
Students should be able to change the subject of a mathematical equation.

In a chemical reaction involving two reactants, it is common to use an excess of one of the reactants to ensure that all of the other reactant is used. The reactant that is completely used up is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products.
Students should be able to explain the effect of a limiting quantity of a reactant on the amount of products it is possible to obtain in terms of amounts in moles or masses in grams.
Many chemical reactions take place in solutions. The concentration of a solution can be measured in mass per given volume of solution, eg grams per dm³ (g/dm³ ).
Students should be able to:
calculate the mass of solute in a given volume of solution of known concentration in terms of mass per given volume of solution
(HT only) explain how the mass of a solute and the volume of a solution is related to the concentration of the solution.

scopeNotes.statement: Many chemical reactions take place in solutions. The concentration of a solution can be measured in mass per given volume of solution, eg grams per dm³ (g/dm³ ).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Concentration is handled here only as mass per given volume of solution, in g/dm³, which is the measure this statement names. No item introduces concentration in mol/dm³, which belongs to 4.8.3, and no item asks for a conversion between the two or for a titration calculation. Every concentration item supplies or asks for a mass of solute in grams and a volume of solution, and volumes given in cm³ are converted to dm³ so that the unit the statement gives is the unit actually used.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) explain how the mass of a solute and the volume of a solution is related to the concentration of the solution.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The explanation item q30, the concept c19 and the misconceptions m20 and m21 are all tiered higher, matching the (HT only) marking on this statement. The rest of 4.3.2.5 - what concentration is, its unit, and calculating the mass of solute in a given volume - is tiered both, so a Foundation student meets only the material 4.3.2.5 asks of them and is never assessed on the explanation reserved for Higher tier.

scopeNotes.statement: The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Relative atomic and relative formula masses are supplied inside the stem of every item that needs one, because working an Mr out from the periodic table is the business of 4.3.1.2, not of this section. Items here test the link between Mr and the mass of one mole, and the use of that link in mole calculations, rather than the arithmetic of building an Mr.

concepts.definition: The unit in which chemical amounts are measured; the symbol for the unit mole is mol. A label such as '0.50 mol of sodium chloride' states a chemical amount, not a mass and not a volume.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass. One mole of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100) has a mass of 100 g; one mole of H₂O (Mr = 18) has a mass of 18 g.

concepts.term: Equal amounts, equal numbers of particles
concepts.definition: One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles - atoms, molecules or ions - as one mole of any other substance. Equal amounts in moles therefore mean equal numbers of particles, however different the masses are.
The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance. Its value is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole. It is a number of particles per mole, not per gram.

Amounts in moles can be applied to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae and equations. In one mole of carbon (C) the number of atoms is the same as the number of molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂), although one mole of CO₂ contains three moles of atoms.
The number of moles in a given mass is found by dividing that mass in grams by the relative formula mass: number of moles = mass ÷ Mr. 20 g of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100) is 0.20 mol.
The mass of a known amount is found by multiplying the amount in moles by the relative formula mass: mass = number of moles x Mr. 0.25 mol of MgCl₂ (Mr = 95) has a mass of 23.75 g.
The masses of reactants and products can be calculated from balanced symbol equations. In a closed system the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants that reacted.

Chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of moles. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ shows that one mole of magnesium reacts with two moles of hydrochloric acid to produce one mole of magnesium chloride and one mole of hydrogen gas.

The balancing numbers in an equation give the ratio of the amounts in moles of the substances involved. They do not give the ratio of the masses, because each substance has its own relative formula mass.

To find the mass of one substance from the mass of another: convert the known mass to moles using its Mr, apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation, then convert back to a mass using the Mr of the substance wanted.

The balancing numbers in a symbol equation can be calculated from the masses of reactants and products by converting the masses in grams to amounts in moles and converting the numbers of moles to simple whole number ratios.

The amounts in moles are divided through by the smallest of them, and multiplied up if needed, so that the balancing numbers are the simplest whole numbers that fit. 0.2 : 0.1 : 0.2 becomes 2 : 1 : 2.
A relationship can be rearranged to make any of its quantities the subject. From number of moles = mass ÷ Mr come mass = number of moles x Mr and Mr = mass ÷ number of moles.
A reactant supplied in more than the amount the equation requires. Using an excess of one reactant makes sure that all of the other reactant is used up.

The reactant that is completely used up in a reaction. It is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products: the amount of product is worked out from the amount of the limiting reactant, not from the reactant in excess.
The concentration of a solution measured as mass per given volume of solution, for example grams per dm³ (g/dm³). A concentration of 20 g/dm³ means 20 g of solute in every 1 dm³ of solution.

concepts.term: Mass of solute in a given volume
concepts.definition: mass of solute = concentration x volume of solution, with the volume in dm³. Because 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, a volume given in cm³ is divided by 1000 before it is used.

Concentration depends on both quantities: for a fixed volume of solution, more solute gives a higher concentration; for a fixed mass of solute, a larger volume of solution gives a lower concentration. Adding water to a solution therefore dilutes it.

misconceptions.question: A bottle is labelled '2 mol of sodium chloride'. Does the label tell you the mass?
misconceptions.correct: No. It gives the chemical amount. The mass is found by multiplying the amount by the relative formula mass, 2 x 58.5 = 117 g.
misconceptions.misconception: A mole is another word for a gram, so 2 mol means 2 g.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everything else a student weighs out in a laboratory is measured in grams, and moles are always introduced alongside masses, so the new unit is absorbed into the familiar one. Writing 'Mr of CO₂ = 44, so one mole is 44 g' invites the reading that mol and g are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: Amount and mass are different quantities with different units. The mole counts particles; the gram measures mass. The relative formula mass is the bridge between them and it is different for every substance.

misconceptions.question: Does one mole of water have the same mass as one mole of sulfur dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. One mole of H₂O has a mass of 18 g and one mole of SO₂ has a mass of 64 g, because their relative formula masses differ.
misconceptions.misconception: One mole of anything has the same mass, because a mole is a fixed quantity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that one mole of any substance contains the same number of particles and then extend 'the same' to mass as well, forgetting that the particles themselves differ in mass.
misconceptions.correction: One mole of any substance contains the same number of the stated particles, but the mass of one mole is numerically equal to the relative formula mass, which is different for each substance.

misconceptions.question: One mole of magnesium has a greater mass than one mole of helium. Does it contain more atoms?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both contain the same number of atoms, 6.02 x 10²³. Magnesium atoms simply have a greater mass than helium atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: A heavier sample must contain more particles, so one mole of magnesium has more atoms than one mole of helium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday life a heavier bag of the same thing does hold more items, and students carry that reasoning across without noticing that the particles being counted are not the same thing at all.
misconceptions.correction: One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles as one mole of any other substance. Extra mass comes from heavier particles, not from more of them.

misconceptions.question: Is the Avogadro constant a number of particles per gram?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance: 6.02 x 10²³ per mole.
misconceptions.misconception: 6.02 x 10²³ is the number of particles in one gram of a substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The constant is met at the same time as the rule linking Mr to grams, so the two 'per' quantities blur together, and the gram is the unit students are more used to.
misconceptions.correction: The Avogadro constant is per mole. The number of particles in one gram is different for every substance and is found by working out the amount in moles first.

misconceptions.question: Is the Avogadro constant 6.02 x 10²² per mole?
misconceptions.correct: No. The value of the Avogadro constant is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole.
misconceptions.misconception: The power of ten in the Avogadro constant is 22, or 24, rather than 23.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The digits 6.02 are memorable while the exponent is not, and standard form is still new, so the index is the part that slips in recall and in copying from a calculator display.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the whole value together: 6.02 x 10²³ per mole. The index is part of the number, and changing it by one changes the value tenfold.

misconceptions.question: Can amounts in moles be used for electrons and ions?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The measurement of amounts in moles can apply to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae and equations.
misconceptions.misconception: Moles can only be used to count atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The mole is introduced with elements and atoms, and the first calculations are all of atoms, so the idea forms that the mole is an atom-counting unit rather than a general counting unit.
misconceptions.correction: The mole counts whatever particle is stated. One mole of electrons, one mole of chloride ions and one mole of water molecules each contain 6.02 x 10²³ of the stated particle.

misconceptions.question: How many moles of atoms are there in one mole of CO₂?
misconceptions.correct: Three moles of atoms: one mole of carbon atoms and two moles of oxygen atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: One mole of CO₂ contains one mole of atoms, because it is one mole of substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'particle' is used loosely, so students stop distinguishing molecules from the atoms inside them and count the formula once rather than counting what it contains.
misconceptions.correction: Read the formula. One mole of CO₂ is one mole of molecules, and each molecule holds three atoms, so it contains three moles of atoms in total.

misconceptions.question: How many moles are there in 20 g of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100)?
misconceptions.misconception: Divide the relative formula mass by the mass, giving 100 ÷ 20 = 5 mol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is remembered as 'divide the two numbers' without which goes on top, and dividing the larger by the smaller feels safer because it avoids an answer below one.
misconceptions.correction: number of moles = mass ÷ Mr. The mass in grams always goes on top. Check the answer against sense: 20 g is less than the 100 g of one mole, so the amount must be less than one mole.

misconceptions.question: What is the mass of one mole of CaCO₃?
misconceptions.correct: 100 g, because the relative formula mass of CaCO₃ is 100 and includes every atom in the formula.
misconceptions.misconception: Use the relative atomic mass of the first element only, giving 40 g for CaCO₃.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol at the front of the formula is the one students look up first, and once a number is found the search stops, especially when subscripts are small and easy to overlook.
misconceptions.correction: The relative formula mass adds the relative atomic mass of every atom shown, including each atom indicated by a subscript: 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100.

misconceptions.question: In Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, what does the 2 in front of HCl mean?
misconceptions.correct: Two moles of hydrochloric acid react with one mole of magnesium.
misconceptions.misconception: The 2 means two grams of HCl.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing numbers are met long before the mole, and in the absence of any other meaning students attach the unit they know best to them.
misconceptions.correction: Balancing numbers are amounts in moles, or numbers of particles. Converting them to masses needs the relative formula mass of each substance.

misconceptions.question: 4.8 g of magnesium reacts completely with 3.2 g of oxygen in a sealed container. What is the mass of magnesium oxide formed?
misconceptions.correct: 8.0 g, the total mass of the reactants that reacted.
misconceptions.misconception: Less than 8.0 g, because gases have hardly any mass or escape during the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In open crucibles and burning experiments mass does appear to change, and gases are treated as weightless in everyday thinking, so conservation is trusted less than the observation.
misconceptions.correction: In a closed system no atoms are gained or lost, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants. The oxygen that reacted still has its mass inside the product.

misconceptions.question: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, is the mass of hydrogen used three times the mass of nitrogen?
misconceptions.correct: No. The 3 gives three moles of H₂ to one mole of N₂, which is 6 g of hydrogen to 28 g of nitrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: The balancing numbers give the ratio of the masses as well as the ratio of the moles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ratios are usually applied to whatever quantity is in front of a student, and moles and masses are both just numbers on the page, so the ratio is transferred without a conversion.
misconceptions.correction: Balancing numbers are a ratio of amounts in moles only. Convert each amount to a mass with its own relative formula mass before comparing masses.

misconceptions.question: 25 g of CaCO₃ is heated and decomposes to CaO and CO₂. What is the mass of CaO formed?
misconceptions.correct: 14 g. 25 g of CaCO₃ is 0.25 mol, which gives 0.25 mol of CaO, and 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass of the product equals the mass of the reactant, so 25 g of CaO is formed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is remembered as 'the mass stays the same', which is true of the total but not of any single substance in a reaction that also gives off a gas.
misconceptions.correction: Total mass is conserved, but it is shared between the products. Work through moles: the CO₂ carries away the rest of the mass.

misconceptions.question: 2.4 g of Mg reacts with 7.3 g of HCl. Can the balancing numbers be read from these masses?
misconceptions.correct: No. Convert each mass to moles first: 0.1 mol of Mg and 0.2 mol of HCl, a ratio of 1 : 2.
misconceptions.misconception: The masses in grams give the balancing numbers directly, so the ratio is 2.4 : 7.3.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The masses are the numbers given in the question, and students look for a ratio in the data in front of them rather than in a quantity they have to calculate for themselves.
misconceptions.correction: Balancing numbers come from amounts in moles. Divide each mass by its own relative formula mass first, then reduce the amounts to a simple whole number ratio.

misconceptions.question: The amounts in a reaction are 0.2 mol of Mg, 0.4 mol of HCl and 0.2 mol of MgCl₂. What are the balancing numbers?
misconceptions.correct: 1, 2 and 1, after dividing through by the smallest amount.
misconceptions.misconception: Multiply the amounts up to give 2Mg + 4HCl → 2MgCl₂ + 2H₂ and leave the equation there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any set of numbers in the right ratio does balance the atoms, so the equation looks correct, and the instruction to reduce to the simplest whole numbers is treated as tidying rather than as part of the answer.
misconceptions.correction: Divide the amounts by the smallest of them so the balancing numbers are the simplest whole numbers that fit. 2 : 4 : 2 : 2 reduces to 1 : 2 : 1 : 1.

misconceptions.question: Starting from number of moles = mass ÷ Mr, how do you make mass the subject?
misconceptions.correct: mass = number of moles x Mr.
misconceptions.misconception: mass = number of moles ÷ Mr, keeping the division that was there before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is done by moving symbols around the page rather than by doing the same operation to both sides, so the operation is copied across unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply both sides by Mr: number of moles x Mr = mass. A quantity that was dividing on one side multiplies when it moves to the other.

misconceptions.question: 0.10 mol of Mg is added to 0.10 mol of HCl. Which is the limiting reactant?
misconceptions.correct: The hydrochloric acid, because Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ needs 0.20 mol of HCl for 0.10 mol of Mg.
misconceptions.misconception: The magnesium, because it has the smaller mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Limiting' sounds like 'least', and mass is the quantity written on the balance, so the smaller mass is read as the smaller amount without any conversion.
misconceptions.correction: Compare amounts in moles against the ratio in the equation, not masses. The reactant that runs out first relative to that ratio is the limiting reactant.

misconceptions.question: Magnesium is burned in a large excess of oxygen. Which reactant fixes the mass of magnesium oxide formed?
misconceptions.correct: The magnesium, which is the limiting reactant.
misconceptions.misconception: The oxygen, because there is much more of it available.
misconceptions.whyItArises: More of something is intuitively linked with more product, so the reactant present in the greater amount is assumed to be in charge of the yield.
misconceptions.correction: The limiting reactant is completely used up and limits the amount of products. Once it has gone the reaction stops, however much of the other reactant is left.

misconceptions.question: The amount of the limiting reactant is doubled while the other reactant stays in excess. What happens to the maximum mass of product?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles, because the amount of product is proportional to the amount of the limiting reactant.
misconceptions.misconception: It stays the same, because the amount of product is fixed by the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The balancing numbers look like fixed quantities of product rather than a ratio, so students treat the yield as a property of the equation instead of a consequence of how much limiting reactant is supplied.
misconceptions.correction: The equation gives a ratio. Twice the amount of limiting reactant gives twice the amount of every product, as long as the other reactant is still in excess.

misconceptions.question: Two solutions each contain 10 g of salt, one in 1 dm³ and one in 2 dm³. Do they have the same concentration?
misconceptions.correct: No. The first is 10 g/dm³ and the second is 5 g/dm³, because concentration depends on the volume as well as the mass.
misconceptions.misconception: Concentration is just how much solute there is, so equal masses mean equal concentrations.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'concentrated' describes a strong-tasting or dark-coloured liquid and is linked to the amount of stuff added, with the volume of liquid left out of the description.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration is a mass per given volume of solution. The same mass of solute in a larger volume of solution gives a lower concentration.

misconceptions.question: Water is added to a solution until its volume doubles. What happens to the concentration?
misconceptions.correct: It halves, because the same mass of solute is now spread through twice the volume of solution.
misconceptions.misconception: The concentration increases, because there is now more solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Adding anything is associated with making a quantity bigger, and students track the total volume rather than the ratio of solute to solution.
misconceptions.correction: Only the volume changes when water is added; the mass of solute is unchanged. Dividing the same mass by a larger volume gives a smaller concentration.

misconceptions.question: What does a concentration of 20 g/dm³ mean?
misconceptions.correct: 20 g of solute is present in every 1 dm³ of solution.
misconceptions.misconception: 20 g of solute is present in every 1 cm³ of solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbols dm³ and cm³ differ by one letter and both are read simply as 'volume', while cm³ is the unit students actually use in the laboratory.
misconceptions.correction: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. A concentration in g/dm³ states the mass of solute in one whole dm³, which is 1000 cm³ of solution.

misconceptions.question: What mass of solute is in 250 cm³ of a solution of concentration 12 g/dm³?
misconceptions.misconception: Multiply 12 by 250 to get 3000 g, using the volume in cm³ as it is given.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The relationship 'mass = concentration x volume' is remembered without the unit it needs, and the volume printed in the question is the number students reach for first.
misconceptions.correction: The volume must be in dm³ to match g/dm³. Divide a volume in cm³ by 1000 before multiplying by the concentration.

misconceptions.question: How many moles are there in 20 g of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100)?
misconceptions.misconception: 2 mol, from dividing 20 by 100 and losing the decimal point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dividing by 100 is done by 'taking off the zeros' rather than by moving the digits two places, and an answer smaller than one looks wrong to a student who expects amounts to be whole.
misconceptions.correction: 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2. Amounts in moles are often less than one; check by asking whether the mass given is more or less than the mass of one mole.

misconceptions.question: How many atoms are there in one mole of water?
misconceptions.correct: Three times the Avogadro constant, because each molecule contains three atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: 6.02 x 10²³ atoms, because one mole of anything contains 6.02 x 10²³ atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Avogadro constant is learned as 'the number in a mole' without the phrase 'of the stated particles', so it is attached to atoms whatever the substance is.
misconceptions.correction: One mole contains 6.02 x 10²³ of the particles stated. For a compound, state whether you are counting formula units, molecules, ions or atoms.

misconceptions.question: How many dm³ is 200 cm³?
misconceptions.correct: 0.2 dm³, because 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
misconceptions.misconception: 2 dm³, dividing by 100 instead of by 1000.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Length conversions from cm to m use 100, and that familiar factor is carried over to a volume conversion where the cube changes the factor.
misconceptions.correction: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. Divide a volume in cm³ by 1000 to get dm³, so 200 cm³ is 0.2 dm³.

misconceptions.question: Can a symbol equation be read in moles?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of moles, so Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ reads as one mole of Mg with two moles of HCl.
misconceptions.misconception: An equation only describes single particles reacting, so its numbers say nothing about laboratory-sized amounts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Equations are first taught with particle diagrams of a few atoms, and the step up to counting particles in moles is a change of scale that is easy to miss.
misconceptions.correction: The same ratio holds at any scale. Multiplying every particle count by 6.02 x 10²³ turns the particle reading into the mole reading.

misconceptions.question: 0.10 mol of Mg is added to 0.10 mol of HCl. Is neither reactant limiting, since the amounts are equal?
misconceptions.correct: No. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ needs twice as much HCl as Mg, so the acid runs out first and is limiting.
misconceptions.misconception: Equal amounts in moles mean neither reactant is limiting, or the one with fewer moles is always the limiting reactant.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Amounts are compared with each other rather than with the ratio the equation requires, so the balancing numbers are left out of the comparison altogether.
misconceptions.correction: Divide each amount by its balancing number and compare. Here 0.10 ÷ 1 for Mg beats 0.10 ÷ 2 for HCl, so the acid is limiting.

misconceptions.question: Concentration = mass of solute ÷ volume of solution. How is the volume made the subject?
misconceptions.correct: volume = mass of solute ÷ concentration.
misconceptions.misconception: volume = mass of solute x concentration, or the mass is made the subject instead of the volume.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is treated as a familiar pattern to be recalled rather than as an operation applied to both sides, so students produce whichever version of the formula triangle they remember best.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply both sides by the volume, then divide both sides by the concentration. Always check that the quantity you wanted is the one left on its own.

misconceptions.question: Is the relative formula mass of CO₂ equal to 44 g?
misconceptions.correct: No. The relative formula mass is 44, a number with no units. The mass of one mole of CO₂ is 44 g.
misconceptions.misconception: Relative formula mass is measured in grams.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The same number appears in both places, and the gram is attached to it as soon as the mass of one mole is met, so the distinction between a relative mass and an actual mass is lost.
misconceptions.correction: Relative formula mass is a ratio and has no unit. It is numerically equal to the mass of one mole in grams, which is where the unit comes from.

mcqs.stem: A bottle in a laboratory is labelled '0.50 mol of sodium chloride'. What does the '0.50 mol' tell you?

options.text: the chemical amount of sodium chloride present
options.rationale: Chemical amounts are measured in moles and mol is the symbol for that unit, so the label states an amount of substance.

options.text: the mass of the sodium chloride, in grams
options.rationale: Students who treat the mole as another name for the gram read the number as a reading from a balance.

options.text: the number of sodium ions in the bottle
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the mole is only ever a raw count of particles of one type.

options.text: the volume the sodium chloride fills
options.rationale: Bottles are usually labelled with volumes, so an unfamiliar unit is assumed to measure space.

mcqs.stem: The relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, is 100. What is the mass of one mole of calcium carbonate?

options.rationale: From dividing the amount by the relative formula mass instead of multiplying, 1 ÷ 100.
The mass of one mole in grams is numerically equal to the relative formula mass, so one mole of CaCO₃ has a mass of 100 g.
From using the relative atomic mass of calcium alone and ignoring the rest of the formula.

options.text: 1 g
options.rationale: From reading 'one mole' as 'one gram'.

mcqs.stem: One mole of water, H₂O (Mr = 18), has a smaller mass than one mole of sulfur dioxide, SO₂ (Mr = 64). Why?

options.text: water is a liquid while sulfur dioxide is a gas
options.rationale: State of matter is the most obvious difference between the two substances, so it is offered as the cause.

options.text: one mole of water contains fewer molecules
options.rationale: Students who link mass to particle number assume the lighter sample must hold fewer particles.

options.text: the relative formula mass of water is smaller
options.rationale: The mass of one mole in grams is numerically equal to the relative formula mass, and 18 is less than 64.

options.text: water molecules are packed more closely
options.rationale: Packing is invoked because the student expects one mole of every substance to have the same mass.

mcqs.stem: A sample holds one mole of magnesium atoms. Another sample holds one mole of helium atoms. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The magnesium sample contains more atoms than the helium.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read a greater mass as a greater number of particles.

options.text: The helium sample contains more atoms, as it is lighter.
options.rationale: The same faulty link between mass and number, applied the other way round.

options.text: The two samples must have the same mass as each other.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who extend 'the same amount' from particle number to mass.

options.text: The two samples contain the same number of atoms.
options.rationale: One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles as one mole of any other substance.

mcqs.stem: What is the value of the Avogadro constant?

options.text: 6.02 x 10²³ particles in one mole
options.rationale: The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole.

options.text: 6.02 x 10²² particles in a mole
options.rationale: The digits are recalled correctly but the power of ten slips by one.

options.text: 6.02 x 10²³ particles per gram
options.rationale: Chosen by students who attach the constant to the gram, the unit they are more used to.

options.text: 6.02 x 10²³ g for every mole
options.rationale: Turns the constant into a mass, confusing it with the rule linking Mr to grams.

mcqs.stem: What does the Avogadro constant tell you?

options.text: the number of particles in one gram of any substance
options.rationale: Swaps the mole for the gram, the unit students meet more often on a balance.

options.text: the number of particles in one mole of a substance
options.rationale: The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance is the Avogadro constant.

options.text: the number of moles in one gram of a substance
options.rationale: Treats the constant as a conversion between grams and moles rather than a particle count.

options.text: the mass in grams of one mole of a substance
options.rationale: Confuses the constant with the numerical link between relative formula mass and grams.

mcqs.stem: In one mole of carbon (C) the number of atoms is the same as the number of molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂). How many moles of atoms are there in one mole of CO₂?

options.text: one mole of atoms, as this is one mole of substance
options.rationale: Counts the formula once instead of counting the atoms the formula contains.

options.text: 44 moles of atoms, from its relative formula mass
options.rationale: Reads the relative formula mass as a number of particles.

options.text: three moles of atoms, one carbon and two oxygen
options.rationale: Each CO₂ molecule holds three atoms, so one mole of molecules contains three moles of atoms.

options.text: two moles of atoms, one for each element present
options.rationale: Counts the elements in the formula rather than the atoms.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about amounts in moles is correct?

options.text: One mole of any solid contains 6.02 x 10²³ atoms.
options.rationale: Applies the constant to atoms whatever the formula, ignoring the phrase 'of the stated particles'.

options.text: Moles can count atoms but not electrons or ions.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who met the mole only with elements and atoms.

options.text: One mole of CO₂ contains one mole of atoms in total.
options.rationale: Counts the formula unit once rather than the three atoms inside it.

options.text: One mole of MgCl₂ contains three moles of ions.
options.rationale: Amounts in moles apply to ions as well as atoms and molecules: one mole of MgCl₂ gives one mole of Mg²⁺ and two moles of Cl⁻.

mcqs.stem: How many moles are there in 20 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ (Mr = 100)?

options.text: 0.20 mol
options.rationale: number of moles = mass ÷ Mr = 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20 mol.

options.text: 5.0 mol
options.rationale: From dividing the relative formula mass by the mass, 100 ÷ 20.

options.text: 20 mol
options.rationale: Reads the mass in grams straight off as an amount in moles.

options.text: 2 mol
options.rationale: The division 20 ÷ 100 is done by cancelling zeros, so the decimal point is lost.

mcqs.stem: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂ (Mr = 95)?

options.rationale: From dividing the amount by the relative formula mass, 0.25 ÷ 95.
mass = number of moles x Mr = 0.25 x 95 = 23.75 g.
From dividing the relative formula mass by the amount, 95 ÷ 0.25.
Gives the mass of one mole and ignores the amount stated in the question.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. In a sealed container, 4.8 g of magnesium reacts completely with 3.2 g of oxygen. Which statement about the magnesium oxide formed is correct?

options.text: It is less than 8.0 g, as some mass is lost as gas.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat gases as weightless or as escaping from a sealed container.

options.text: It is 4.8 g, since only the magnesium is weighed out.
options.rationale: Assumes the product has the same mass as the solid reactant supplied.

options.text: It is 8.0 g, the total mass of the reactants.
options.rationale: Mass is conserved in a closed system, so 4.8 g + 3.2 g of reactants give 8.0 g of magnesium oxide.

options.text: It is 3.2 g, the mass of the oxygen that reacted.
options.rationale: Picks the other reactant mass, again equating a single reactant with the product.

mcqs.stem: The equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O can be interpreted in terms of moles. Which reading of it is correct?

options.text: Two grams of H₂ react with one gram of O₂ gas.
options.rationale: Attaches grams to the balancing numbers instead of moles.

options.text: Two moles of H₂ react with two moles of O₂.
options.rationale: Copies the coefficient of the product across to the oxygen without reading the equation.

options.text: Two molecules of H₂ give one molecule of H₂O.
options.rationale: The particle reading is attempted but misapplied: two H₂ molecules give two H₂O molecules.

options.text: Two moles of H₂ react with one mole of O₂.
options.rationale: The balancing numbers give the amounts in moles: two moles of hydrogen to one mole of oxygen.

mcqs.stem: The equation Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ is given in the specification. Which statement does it show?

options.text: One mole of Mg reacts with two moles of HCl.
options.rationale: The balancing numbers show one mole of magnesium reacting with two moles of hydrochloric acid.

options.text: A gram of Mg reacts with two grams of HCl.
options.rationale: Reads the balancing numbers as masses in grams.

options.text: One mole of Mg reacts with one mole of HCl.
options.rationale: Ignores the 2 in front of HCl and assumes a one-to-one ratio.

options.text: Two moles of Mg react with a mole of HCl.
options.rationale: Attaches the balancing number to the wrong substance.

mcqs.stem: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What mass of magnesium chloride (Mr = 95) is produced when 2.4 g of magnesium (Ar = 24) reacts completely?

options.rationale: From dividing the mass of magnesium by the Mr of the product, 2.4 ÷ 95.
2.4 ÷ 24 = 0.1 mol of Mg, which gives 0.1 mol of MgCl₂, and 0.1 x 95 = 9.5 g.
The amount 2.4 ÷ 24 is written as 0.01 mol, so the answer comes out ten times too small.
Gives the mass of one mole of MgCl₂ without using the amount of magnesium supplied.

mcqs.stem: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What mass of calcium oxide (Mr = 56) is produced when 25 g of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) decomposes completely?

options.rationale: From dividing the amount in moles by the Mr instead of multiplying, 0.25 ÷ 56.
From dividing the mass given by the Mr of the product, 25 ÷ 56.
25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol of CaCO₃ gives 0.25 mol of CaO, and 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.
From inverting the first step, 100 ÷ 25 = 4 mol, then 4 x 56.

mcqs.stem: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What mass of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) must be heated to produce 5.6 g of calcium oxide (Mr = 56)?

options.rationale: From dividing the mass of product by the Mr of the reactant, 5.6 ÷ 100.
Stops at the amount in moles and writes it as though it were a mass in grams.
Assumes the mass of reactant equals the mass of the product formed.
5.6 ÷ 56 = 0.1 mol of CaO, so 0.1 mol of CaCO₃ is needed, and 0.1 x 100 = 10 g.

mcqs.stem: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, one mole of nitrogen reacts with three moles of hydrogen. Why is the mass of hydrogen used not three times the mass of nitrogen?

options.text: the balancing numbers give a ratio of moles, not of masses
options.rationale: Each amount must be converted to a mass using its own relative formula mass, so the mass ratio is 6 g to 28 g.

options.text: the mass ratio is the same as the mole ratio in all cases
options.rationale: Denies the premise of the question by transferring the ratio straight to masses.

options.text: some of the hydrogen escapes before it is able to react
options.rationale: Explains the difference by loss of gas rather than by relative formula mass.

options.text: hydrogen molecules are smaller than nitrogen molecules
options.rationale: Uses particle size in place of the numerical relationship between moles and mass.

mcqs.stem: The masses of the reactants and products in a reaction are known. How are the balancing numbers in the symbol equation found?

options.text: use the ratio of the masses in grams as the numbers
options.rationale: Takes the ratio from the data given without converting the masses to amounts.

options.text: convert each mass to moles, then find the simplest ratio
options.rationale: Masses in grams are converted to amounts in moles, and those amounts are converted to simple whole number ratios.

options.text: divide each mass by the number of atoms in the formula
options.rationale: Uses atom counts in place of relative formula masses.

options.text: multiply each mass by its relative formula mass
options.rationale: Uses the right quantity but the wrong operation when converting to moles.

mcqs.stem: 4.0 g of hydrogen (Mr of H₂ = 2), 32 g of oxygen (Mr of O₂ = 32) and 36 g of water (Mr of H₂O = 18) are measured in a reaction. Which balanced equation fits these masses?

options.text: 2H₂ + 2O₂ → 2H₂O
options.rationale: Keeps the hydrogen and water coefficients but makes the oxygen match them, so the atoms no longer balance.

options.text: 2H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
options.rationale: The reactant amounts are converted but the amount of product is left as one.

options.text: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
options.rationale: 4.0 ÷ 2 = 2 mol H₂, 32 ÷ 32 = 1 mol O₂ and 36 ÷ 18 = 2 mol H₂O, a ratio of 2 : 1 : 2.

options.text: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
options.rationale: Chosen by students who write the formulae without converting any mass to moles.

mcqs.stem: 2.4 g of magnesium (Ar = 24) reacts with 7.3 g of hydrochloric acid (Mr of HCl = 36.5) to give 9.5 g of magnesium chloride (Mr = 95) and 0.2 g of hydrogen (Mr of H₂ = 2). Which equation fits these masses?

options.text: 2Mg + 4HCl → 2MgCl₂ + 2H₂
options.rationale: The ratio is right but it has not been reduced to the simplest whole numbers.

options.text: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂
options.rationale: The acid is converted correctly but the hydrogen coefficient is copied from it.

options.text: Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
options.rationale: Assumes a one-to-one ratio without converting the masses to moles.

options.text: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
options.rationale: 0.1 mol Mg, 0.2 mol HCl, 0.1 mol MgCl₂ and 0.1 mol H₂ give the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 : 1.

mcqs.stem: The amount of a substance is found from number of moles = mass ÷ Mr. To make mass the subject of this relationship, what should you do?

options.text: Multiply the number of moles by the Mr.
options.rationale: Multiplying both sides by Mr leaves mass on its own, giving mass = number of moles x Mr.

options.text: Multiply the mass by the number of moles.
options.rationale: Rearranges for the wrong subject, and multiplies two quantities that are never multiplied together.

options.text: Divide the Mr by the number of moles.
options.rationale: Divides the wrong way round, a common slip when symbols are moved rather than operations applied.

options.text: Divide the number of moles by Mr.
options.rationale: Keeps the division that was in the original relationship instead of reversing it.

mcqs.stem: Concentration = mass of solute ÷ volume of solution. A student knows the concentration and the volume and needs the mass of solute. What should they do?

options.text: Multiply the concentration by 1000 cm³ first.
options.rationale: Reaches for a unit conversion instead of rearranging, and applies it to the wrong quantity.

options.text: Multiply the concentration by the volume.
options.rationale: Multiplying both sides by the volume makes the mass of solute the subject.

options.text: Divide the concentration by the volume used.
options.rationale: Keeps the division from the original relationship instead of reversing it.

options.text: Divide the volume by the concentration.
options.rationale: Not a valid rearrangement at all. Dividing the mass of solute by the concentration is what gives the volume, and the volume is not what is wanted here.

mcqs.stem: In a reaction between two reactants, what is meant by the limiting reactant?

options.text: the reactant that is added in excess
options.rationale: Swaps the two terms, taking the excess reactant to be the one in control.

options.text: the reactant with the smallest mass used
options.rationale: Reads 'limiting' as 'least by mass' without converting to amounts in moles.

options.text: the reactant that is completely used up
options.rationale: The reactant that is completely used up is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products.

options.text: the reactant that is left over at the end
options.rationale: Describes the reactant in excess rather than the one that runs out.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. A student adds 0.10 mol of magnesium to 0.10 mol of hydrochloric acid. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The magnesium is limiting, as it has the smaller mass.
options.rationale: 0.10 mol of Mg is 2.4 g against 3.65 g of HCl, so a comparison of masses points the wrong way.

options.text: Neither reactant is limiting, as the amounts match.
options.rationale: Compares the amounts with each other instead of with the ratio in the equation.

options.text: The magnesium is the limiting reactant in this mixture.
options.rationale: Assumes the reactant named first, or the solid, must be the one used up.

options.text: The hydrochloric acid is the limiting reactant.
options.rationale: 0.10 mol of Mg needs 0.20 mol of HCl, so the acid runs out first and the magnesium is in excess.

mcqs.stem: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 0.20 mol of magnesium is burned in 0.50 mol of oxygen. Which statement is correct?

options.text: 0.20 mol of MgO forms, as the magnesium is limiting
options.rationale: 0.20 mol of Mg needs only 0.10 mol of O₂, so the magnesium is used up and gives 0.20 mol of MgO.

options.text: 0.50 mol of MgO forms, since the oxygen is in excess
options.rationale: Works the answer out from the reactant in excess instead of the limiting one.

options.text: 0.70 mol of MgO forms, using up both the reactants
options.rationale: Adds the two amounts, assuming every mole supplied ends up in the product.

options.text: 0.10 mol of MgO forms, from the 2 in the equation
options.rationale: Divides by the balancing number a second time after it has already been used.

mcqs.stem: A reaction is repeated with twice as much of the limiting reactant, while the other reactant is still in excess. What happens to the maximum mass of product?

options.text: It stays the same, as the equation fixes the amount formed.
options.rationale: Treats the balancing numbers as fixed quantities rather than as a ratio.

options.text: It doubles, as the limiting reactant sets the amount formed.
options.rationale: The amount of product is proportional to the amount of the limiting reactant while the other is in excess.

options.text: It halves, because the excess reactant is now shared out.
options.rationale: Makes the excess reactant control the yield, so more of the other seems to dilute it.

options.text: It is unchanged until the excess reactant is doubled.
options.rationale: Again gives the reactant in excess the controlling role.

mcqs.stem: A solution has a concentration of 20 g/dm³. What does this tell you?

options.text: there is 20 g of solute in each 1 cm³ of solution
options.rationale: Reads dm³ as cm³, the unit used on laboratory glassware.

options.text: there is 20 g of solute, whatever the volume may be
options.rationale: Drops the volume from the definition and treats concentration as a mass.

options.text: there is 20 g of solute in every 1 dm³ of solution
options.rationale: Concentration measured in g/dm³ is a mass per given volume of solution, here 20 g in each dm³.

options.text: there is 20 g of solvent in 1 dm³ of solute
options.rationale: Swaps solute and solvent, a confusion of terms rather than of arithmetic.

mcqs.stem: A solution has a concentration of 12 g/dm³. What mass of solute is present in 250 cm³ of this solution?

options.rationale: From dividing the concentration by the volume in cm³, 12 ÷ 250.
From multiplying by the volume in cm³ without converting it to dm³.
From dividing by the volume in dm³ instead of multiplying, 12 ÷ 0.25.
250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³, and mass = concentration x volume = 12 x 0.25 = 3.0 g.

mcqs.stem: A student needs 7.5 g of a solute. The solution available has a concentration of 25 g/dm³. What volume of the solution should be measured out?

options.text: 300 cm³
options.rationale: volume = mass ÷ concentration = 7.5 ÷ 25 = 0.3 dm³, and 0.3 x 1000 = 300 cm³.
From multiplying the mass by the concentration instead of dividing.

options.text: 0.30 cm³
options.rationale: The volume 0.3 dm³ is found correctly but is never converted into cm³.

options.text: 30 cm³
options.rationale: The conversion from dm³ to cm³ uses 100 rather than 1000.

mcqs.stem: A solution contains 4.0 g of solute in 200 cm³ of solution. Water is added until the volume of the solution is 400 cm³. What happens to the concentration?

options.text: It rises from 20 g/dm³ to 40 g/dm³, as more has been added.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'adding' as 'making more concentrated'.

options.text: It falls from 20 g/dm³ to 10 g/dm³, as the volume doubles.
options.rationale: The mass of solute stays at 4.0 g while the volume doubles to 0.4 dm³, so 4.0 ÷ 0.4 = 10 g/dm³.

options.text: It stays at 20 g/dm³, as the mass of solute is fixed.
options.rationale: Treats concentration as depending on the mass of solute alone.

options.text: It falls from 2.0 g/dm³ to 1.0 g/dm³, halving as water goes in.
options.rationale: The direction is right but 200 cm³ is converted to dm³ by dividing by 100.
